title: Sowing leeks
subtitle: Indoor sowing from January for transplanting in May and June
excerpt: Leeks are sown indoors from January to March and transplanted as pencil-thick seedlings into deep holes in May or June. They need a long growing season; a January sowing gives the best autumn and winter crop.
sourceNotes: Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), kitchen garden section. RHS leek growing guide (rhs.org.uk). USDA cooperative extension notes on allium crops, public domain. Joy Larkcom, Grow Your Own Vegetables, public-domain passages on leek transplanting.

glossaryTerms.definition: Covering the lower stem of a leek to exclude light, producing a longer white shank. Achieved by planting in a deep hole (6 to 10 cm deep), by earthing soil up around the stem as the plant grows, or by fitting a collar around the stem. The white blanched section is the edible part most valued in cooking.

The traditional leek transplanting method: make a 10 cm deep hole with a dibber, drop the bare-rooted seedling in so the roots reach the bottom, then pour water into the hole without filling it with soil. The water carries some soil around the roots; the hole gradually fills with soil as the plant grows. This gives the deep planting that blanches the stem.

content.text: Leeks need a long season: sow indoors in January or February, transplant into their final position in May or June, and harvest from September through to March. A January sowing gives the longest season and the best winter crop. The seedlings go into deep holes to

Sow indoors from January to mid-March. A heated propagator gives the earliest germination in January; from February onwards a warm windowsill is sufficient. Sowing after mid-March gives a smaller, less well-blanched leek harvested from October rather than September.

Sow in module trays or a seed tray filled with seed compost. Scatter seed thinly over the surface and cover with 1 cm of compost. Keep at 15 to 18°C for germination: a heated propagator for January sowings, a warm room from February. Once seedlings emerge, move to a bright cool windowsill to prevent them going leggy.

In seed trays: sow 1 cm deep, 1 cm apart in rows 5 cm apart. Prick out into modules (6 to 9 cm) when seedlings are 5 cm tall. Grow on until stems are 6 to 8 mm thick (pencil thickness), usually 8 to 12 weeks after sowing. Transplant into final positions with 20 cm between plants and 30 cm between rows.

Leek seedlings emerge as a thin single curled shoot that straightens as it grows. Germination takes one to two weeks at 15 to 18°C. The seedlings look like short green blades of grass for the first month. Prick out or thin them when they have one true leaf beyond the seed leaf.
Transplant in May or June when the seedlings are pencil-thick. Water the modules or tray well the night before to ease removal. Use a dibber to make holes 10 cm deep and 20 cm apart.

without filling the hole with soil. The plant will anchor itself as it grows.

attrs.heading: Common problems
attrs.intro: What goes wrong most often with leek sowing and transplanting.

items.symptom: Seedlings thin and leggy after germination
items.cause: Insufficient light, too warm, or sown too thickly.
items.fix: Move to the brightest available position. Thin if overcrowded. Prick out early and give each seedling its own module.

items.symptom: Transplants fail to establish and flop
items.cause: Roots dried out before planting, or planted too shallow.
items.fix: Trim roots to 3 cm before planting; water in immediately. Plant into a 10 cm hole, not a shallow trench.

items.symptom: Orange pustules or rust-coloured streaks on leaves in autumn
items.cause: Leek rust (Puccinia allii), a fungal disease worse in wet seasons.
items.fix: Remove affected leaves. Increase spacing to improve air circulation. Rust rarely kills leeks; plants are still edible with rust removed. Grow rust-resistant varieties such as Bandit or Apollo for next season.
